NJ Lt. Gov. Caldwell Resigns After Sexual Harassment Probe
sources.text:
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill's hand-picked lieutenant governor resigned under pressure after an independent investigation substantiated sexual harassment and repeated ethics violations, a scandal that now raises pointed questions about accountability inside her own administration.
Sherrill, a Democrat, gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell a 24-hour ultimatum on Thursday to step down after investigators concluded he made a sexually charged remark to a female staffer, used his office to push a promotion for his romantic partner, and brought unpaid personal guests to at least seven ticketed state events. Caldwell submitted his resignation but denied every finding, telling the New York Times he was leaving only to avoid becoming "a distraction to the administration."
The 61-page report, led by former New Jersey Attorney General Christopher Porrino, did not find Caldwell's denials persuasive. Investigators concluded his claim that he never made the offending remark to the staffer "was not credible." The probe also found Caldwell continued the very conduct under scrutiny, bringing guests to events without ethics clearance or payment, the day after he was formally told he was under investigation.
The ethics investigation began after the state's chief ethics officer received an anonymous complaint in May alleging inappropriate behavior toward women and policy violations. Caldwell was formally notified on May 22. What happened next did not suggest a man taking the matter seriously.
On May 23, one day later, Caldwell brought personal guests to a ticketed event without advance clearance or payment, a practice investigators said he had been warned about repeatedly through prior training. Four days after notification, he used his state email to recommend his romantic partner for a leadership position in another executive branch department, forwarding her resume and letter of interest. He referred to her as "my friend" and did not disclose the romantic relationship.
Investigators described the pattern as ongoing despite multiple warnings. The report also found Caldwell had tasked a staffer with finding him a "first lady," the New York Post reported, adding another layer to the portrait of an official who treated his public office as a personal concierge service.
The sexual harassment finding centered on a remark Caldwell made to a female aide. Investigators found he told her: "you young women are looking for young sperm." The comment came after the staffer told Caldwell her younger friend was not interested in a romantic relationship with him. The staffer subsequently tried to distance herself from Caldwell at work and avoid traveling with him when possible.
Sherrill framed the resignation demand as a matter of institutional integrity. In a statement, she said the findings were "extremely troubling" and described Caldwell's conduct as "a pattern of behavior" that persisted despite warnings and training.
Fox News Digital reported that Sherrill declared the resignation "necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents." She added that she would not accept "a culture that sweeps misconduct under the rug" in New Jersey, a standard her critics may now measure against her own vetting process.
Sherrill could not fire Caldwell directly. Under New Jersey's constitution, only the state legislature can remove a lieutenant governor through impeachment. Just The News reported that Sherrill warned impeachment proceedings could follow if Caldwell refused to step down.
Caldwell chose to resign but made clear he was not conceding the substance. His attorney, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the investigation's conclusions directly, stating: "The question is whether the evidence actually proves that a violation occurred. In our view, the evidence does not support these findings."
Caldwell himself went further, attributing the investigation to racial bias, a claim the report does not appear to address, based on available reporting. He told the New York Times his departure was not about the findings but about sparing the administration further distraction.
In a move that drew attention for its timing, Sherrill used her announcement to take a swipe at President Trump, claiming he "continues to undermine confidence in public service at the federal level." The remark landed oddly in context. The misconduct at issue occurred entirely within Sherrill's own administration, carried out by a lieutenant governor she personally selected as her running mate, a man she once praised as "a voice for the voiceless."
Sherrill's administration has faced scrutiny on other fronts as well. Her handling of this scandal comes as she has simultaneously clashed with the Trump Justice Department over voter data. Sherrill has refused to hand over noncitizen voter records to federal investigators, even as her own state acknowledged the scope of the problem.
New Jersey officials have admitted that 6,600 non-citizens ended up on the state's voter rolls, a disclosure that prompted the RNC to put election officials on notice. Those controversies paint a picture of a governor eager to lecture Washington on standards while struggling to enforce them closer to home.
The Washington Examiner reported that Sherrill characterized the investigation's findings as showing "serious, repeated violations of state policy" in which Caldwell "failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office." She also said she holds everyone in her administration "to the highest ethical standard" and that "anyone who violates these will be held accountable."
Caldwell's resignation closes one chapter but opens several uncomfortable questions for Sherrill. The governor commissioned the investigation roughly three months before the findings were released, meaning her office was aware of the allegations for an extended period before acting publicly. How Caldwell passed the vetting process to become her running mate in the first place remains unexplained.
Fox News Digital reached out to Caldwell for comment on the report and Sherrill's demand but did not receive a response at the time of publication. Caldwell's only public statements came through his attorney and his remarks to the New York Times.
The full 61-page report has not been made publicly available, and the identity of the anonymous complainant who triggered the probe remains undisclosed. Whether the state legislature will pursue any further action against Caldwell now that he has resigned is also unclear. New Jersey's political landscape is already crowded with unresolved accountability questions, this episode adds one more.
When a governor has to publicly demand that her own hand-picked deputy resign over sexual harassment and ethics violations, the failure is not just his. It belongs to the administration that chose him, vouched for him, and now wants credit for showing him the door.

NEW JERSEY LT. GOV. CALDWELL RESIGNS AFTER SHERRILL DEMANDS HE STEP DOWN OVER HARASSMENT FINDINGS
sources.text:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale G. Caldwell resigned his office Friday afternoon after Gov. Mikie Sherrill publicly demanded he step down, saying an independent investigation had documented serious and repeated violations of state policy.
The resignation was reported across multiple outlets within the span of about an hour. The Washington Times wrote at 8:39 p.m. UTC that "New Jersey Democratic Lt. Gov. Dale G. Caldwell has resigned following a bombshell ethics and sexual harassment inquiry." CNN, at 8:06 p.m., reported that "New Jersey's Democratic lieutenant governor has resigned after the governor demanded he step down over sexual harassment allegations and ethical lapses involving his relationships with women," adding that Caldwell "has denied any misconduct." ABC News, at 7:19 p.m., said Caldwell "resigned Friday as lieutenant governor of New Jersey after an investigation found 'serious, repeated violations of state policy, including ethical lapses and a substantiated finding of sexual harassment,' NJ Gov. Mikie Sherrill said." Fox News, at 7:08 p.m., broke the resignation as well, and OANN, at 7:36 p.m., reported that Caldwell "has agreed to resign after Gov. Mikie Sherrill called for him to step down following the release of an independent ethics investigation," describing a sixty-one-page report.
The sequence began earlier in the day, before the resignation. The Gateway Pundit wrote at 7:30 p.m. UTC that "New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is demanding the resignation of Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell after an independent ethics investigation found serious violations of state policy, including a substantiated sexual harassment allegation," and that "Sherrill gave Caldwell until Friday to resign."
Sherrill made the demand in remarks carried on camera and posted by Fox News. In words the network quoted directly, the governor said: "Yesterday, I called for Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell to resign, following the release of the independent investigation into his conduct. As outlined in the report, the investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office, and he demonstrated a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this administration. The report documents serious, repeated violations of state policy, including ethical lapses and a substantiated finding of sexual harassment. I gave the Lieutenant Governor until today to resign. He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted."
According to reporting by The New York Times, investigators found that the lieutenant governor sought a promotion for his girlfriend and made a sexually charged comment to a staff member. Politico described a months-long investigation that found Caldwell engaged in behavior that "constituted sexual harassment" along with ethics violations; Caldwell denied wrongdoing, the outlet reported. Gothamist reported that Sherrill said it is "in the best interest" of Garden State residents for Caldwell to step down, after a report confirmed what the outlet described as scathing allegations of inappropriate comments made by him.
Other local coverage tracked the same timeline. 6abc Philadelphia reported that Sherrill called on Caldwell to resign following the release of the independent investigation's findings, and Politico, in a later story about the resignation itself, reported that Caldwell stepped down under pressure not only from the governor but from fellow Democrats.
The accounts carrying the story Friday evening spanned the ideological range of national political media: the Washington Times, CNN, ABC News, Fox News, OANN, the Gateway Pundit, Politico, the New York Times, Gothamist and 6abc Philadelphia all reported on the demand or the resignation, or both. The same basic elements recurred across them — the independent investigation, the substantiated sexual harassment finding, the ethical lapses, the deadline Sherrill set, and the resignation she accepted.
As described in that coverage, the underlying claims against Caldwell rest on the findings of an independent ethics investigation, not on an outside court proceeding or an admission by Caldwell himself. Caldwell has denied any misconduct, according to CNN and Politico, and no outlet reported a criminal charge against him in connection with the findings.
Next News Network could not independently verify the findings of the investigation or the underlying allegations against Caldwell.
What happens next is not yet known. The investigation report has been released and Sherrill has accepted the resignation. Whether Caldwell, who is sixty-one according to OANN, will face any further proceedings, and who will fill the lieutenant governor's office for the remainder of the term, were not specified in the accounts reviewed Friday evening. Neither the governor's office nor Caldwell issued any additional statement in the material available at the time of publication beyond the exchange described by the outlets above.
Our Take
The resignation is the headline, but the more telling part of this story is the speed. Sherrill released the report, set a deadline, and by Friday afternoon the man who was one heartbeat from her office was gone. That is what accountability looks like when a party decides it would rather lose a lieutenant governor than spend months defending one.
Compare that reaction to the pattern we have watched play out again and again in statehouses and in Washington. When the accused is from the other party, Democrats find no shortage of ways to explain why the process needs to run its course, why the report is disputed, why the voters should decide. When the report is sitting on their own desk and the cameras are rolling, the standard suddenly gets very clear. That is not a complaint about the outcome here, which is the right one. It is a reminder for readers to keep the same standard in mind the next time the name in the headline belongs to the other side.
The caution that matters today is different. The findings rest on an independent investigation, and Caldwell has denied wrongdoing. We reported that plainly, and we flagged that we could not verify the allegations ourselves. That is what a news organization is supposed to do — report what those in a position to know are saying, name them, and let readers weigh it. The networks that spent years telling their audience that the mere existence of an investigation proves guilt will now discover, in this case, that the accused deserves a presumption of innocence. Both things can be true at once: the report is serious, and the man still gets to deny it.
What New Jersey voters should take from this is less about Caldwell than about the system above him. A lieutenant governor with a substantiated harassment finding sat one step from the governorship until an unrelated political moment forced the issue. The vetting failed long before the investigation began. If Sherrill's administration wants credit for acting quickly, it should also explain how someone with this record reached the state's second-highest office in the first place.

sources.text:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned from his position following an investigation that found he violated state ethics and harassment policy, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Friday at a press conference.
“He submitted his resignation to me this afternoon, which I accepted,” Sherrill said. Caldwell was not present at the announcement.
On Thursday, Sherrill urged Caldwell’s resignation after releasing a report summarizing the findings of a probe of his behavior conducted by a law firm hired by the state, which found evidence that he violated ethics rules by committing sexual harassment.
In a statement Thursday, Sherrill said that Caldwell, a fellow Democrat, “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.”
Caldwell’s resignation, she added, “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.”
Investigators said in the 61-page report that they found credible evidence that Caldwell violated workplace policy “in his conduct by commenting to a female staffer that young women want ‘young sperm.’”
They also found he violated an ethics code and code of conduct “when he brought guests to ticketed events without payment or reimbursement” and “when he sought to obtain a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship.”
Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.”
“This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Caldwell’s attorney Thomas Calcagni.
Calcagni didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.
On Friday, Sherrill pushed back on Calcagni’s criticism of the investigation, saying: “I think it’s very thorough. It lays out exactly what the investigation looked into.” She added that Caldwell’s own statements were included in the report, saying, “So, obviously he was fully involved in this as well.”
Sherrill also defended having Caldwell step in as acting governor on several occasions after the investigation began, saying, “As a former federal prosecutor, it is important to me that everyone have a fair hearing.”
“Once I saw those complaints, once I saw the findings of that investigation, I acted quickly and asked for the resignation of the lieutenant governor,” Sherrill said.
The governor said her demand that Caldwell step down is part of her efforts to dismantle a culture that ignores victims.
“There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug,” Sherrill said. “That is not the kind of government I’m running. When I say there is a culture change taking place, I mean it. This is part of it.”
New Jersey state Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin, a Democrat, applauded Sherrill for her “commitment to hold public officials to the highest standards.”
“Following an independent investigation, Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell was right to resign from office today,” Coughlin said in a statement. “We must ensure the work of governing is uninterrupted and that serving the people of New Jersey remains a top priority.”
Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, an office that oversees elections.
Sherrill said Friday that the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, would become acting secretary of state with just weeks to go until the midterm elections.
“Shirley is a veteran of the U.S. Department of Justice and the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office,” Sherrill said. “She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting.”
The lieutenant governor’s duties also include filling in for the governor when she leaves the state. Sherrill said that until a new lieutenant governor is in place, there is “an order of command” for who would step in for her during any absence, beginning with the state Senate president.
Under New Jersey law, the lieutenant governor must be replaced within 45 days of the position becoming vacant. Sherrill said she would “certainly” make a permanent appointment within that time frame but does not plan on naming an acting lieutenant governor in the meantime.
“We will be making sure with our chief counsel that we’re following the rules,” Sherrill said. “This is a little bit of a new area for New Jersey, so we’re going to ensure that we get legal opinions and follow the process there.”

"His decision will allow us to move forward with important work serving the people of our state," she said. "In my administration we are committed to doing what is right, not what is politically expedient."

Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigns after report cites ethics violations
Lt. Gov. Caldwell stepped down after a report found he made crass remarks to subordinates and tried to get a girlfriend a new state job. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned, less than 24 hours after the Sherrill administration released a bombshell report accusing Caldwell of sexual harassment and multiple ethical lapses.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Caldwell submitted his resignation Friday afternoon and she accepted it.
“Public service, holding the public trust, is a privilege, not a right. I feel deeply that it is a commitment by elected officials to serve the people, not their own self-interest,” Sherrill (D) told reporters at the Statehouse in Trenton Friday. “To honor that commitment, public servants must abide by the highest ethical standards. Those standards apply to everyone, regardless of their title.”
Caldwell (D), who was elected along with Sherrill in November and took office in January, made crass remarks to women subordinates, repeatedly attempted to get a promotion for a state worker he was dating, and took uninvited guests to seven ticketed events without permission or payment, the report released Thursday says.
The findings came four months after an anonymous ethics complaint drove Sherrill to enlist former New Jersey Attorney General Chris Porrino to conduct an independent investigation. Asked whether she would refer his findings to the attorney general’s office or any other authorities, Sherrill said she had been focused on getting Caldwell out of office, and her administration would determine later whether to push for further penalties.
Caldwell has denied wrongdoing.
Shirley Emehelu, the state comptroller, will replace Caldwell as secretary of state.
“We are just 39 days away from the midterm elections,” Sherrill said. “It is of paramount importance that our elections run smoothly and that New Jerseyans have confidence in the officials overseeing them.”
Voters concerned about what impact the leadership change might have on election integrity should worry more about President Donald Trump, Sherrill added.
“I have deep concerns about all the ways the President will try to use his federal power to undermine our elections. He has been attempting to get access to our voter rolls and private voter data since I took office,” Sherrill said.
Emehelu, who stood at Sherrill’s side Friday, said she has more than two decades of experience upholding the rule of law in her previous jobs at the U.S. Department of Justice and the state Attorney General’s Office.
“Even though the leadership might look different, Governor Sherrill’s commitment is the same. New Jersey elections will be conducted freely, fairly, and with integrity. Every eligible voter will have the chance to cast a ballot, and every legal ballot will be counted,” Emelehu said.
Sherrill said she would name a new lieutenant governor within the next 45 days, someone with “a dedication to the people of New Jersey” who is “focused on the public good.”
“This is a little bit of a new area for New Jersey, so we’re going to ensure that we get legal opinions and follow the process there,” she said.
The Legislature’s Democratic leaders welcomed Caldwell’s resignation as “the right thing to do.”
“Continued service would hinder the effective execution of the duties assigned to the Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State,” said Sen. Nicholas Scutari (D-Union), who is Senate president. “Stepping down is in the best interests of our residents and the integrity of public office.”
Assemblyman Craig Coughlin (D-Middlesex), who serves as Assembly speaker, seconded Scutari.
“We must ensure the work of governing is uninterrupted and that serving the people of New Jersey remains a top priority,” Coughlin said. “I support Governor Sherrill’s commitment to hold public officials to the highest standards and her work to bring this matter to a swift resolution, enabling us to move forward in the best interests of the state.”
Republicans applauded Caldwell’s departure too, but Senate Republican Leader Anthony Bucco (R-Morris) said questions remain and that the Sherrill administration should release all investigatory records with minimal redactions.
“This administration has been mired in chaos from the start and has lacked transparency in its conduct. But now that the Lieutenant Governor has agreed to resign, there is no reason to hide behind secrecy. The public deserves full disclosure. All records, reports, and internal communications related to these allegations and the investigation should be made available to the public as soon as possible,” Bucco said. “The public has a right to know.”
The Assembly’s Republican leader, John DiMaio, also blasted Sherrill’s “failure to vet the man she chose to stand one heartbeat from the governorship” and proposed that whoever Sherrill picks to replace Caldwell get an OK from legislators first.
“She announced Caldwell as her running mate 45 days after the primary. Now she has 45 days to choose his replacement,” DiMaio said. “To avoid another disaster, Sherrill should ask her choice to appear publicly before Senate and Assembly committees. The appointment does not require legislative confirmation, but after Caldwell, the governor cannot expect New Jerseyans to simply take her word that she got the vetting right this time.”
Sherrill dismissed Republicans’ criticism as sour grapes.
“I think members of the GOP are not happy because they’ve had to duck and cover for years now, because the President of the United States, the head of their party, is the most corrupt individual in politics, has enriched himself to the tune of billions of dollars, is raising gas prices about $5 a barrel, and because of a war that he can’t explain, can’t get out of, he continues to try to steal an election,” she said. “They’re probably unhappy because we are running an incredibly competent government here in New Jersey, which I think stands in such sharp contrast to everything we see at the federal level.”
She said Caldwell’s investigation and resignation should reassure the public that she’s intent on making a “culture change” in state government.
“There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug. You can speak to numerous people who’ve worked in the Statehouse for decades, who felt this day would never come, that allegations would never be taken seriously, action would never be taken, and victims would just have to either quit their job or move on. That is not the kind of government I’m running,” Sherrill said.

sources.text:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigns after investigation found sexual harassment and other wrongdoing
Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell's resignation comes the day after N.J. Gov. Mikie Sherrill called on him to do so. She says she'll act swiftly to find a new No. 2.
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned after investigators found “credible evidence” of sexual harassment and other wrongdoing.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced his resignation at a news conference Friday afternoon after calling for him to step down while releasing the investigative report Thursday evening.
“His decision will allow us to move forward with important work serving the people of our state,” said Sherrill, who was inaugurated with Caldwell by her side in January.
“I will move swiftly and thoughtfully in choosing a new lieutenant governor who will represent my administration and the people of New Jersey with honor and integrity.”
The governor released a 61-page report from a monthlong investigation conducted by an outside law firm late Thursday afternoon. The report said Caldwell made inappropriate comments to women and violated ethics rules. Caldwell, a minister, is the former president of Centenary University.
Sherrill called for him to resign by Friday, but it was unclear whether he would listen. Caldwell denied the investigation’s findings through his attorney, who argued Caldwell was not given an opportunity to meaningfully address the accusations in the report or provide his own witnesses.
Sherrill emphasized Friday that she wanted to “make sure everyone was treated fairly and justly” and called the investigation thorough and impartial.
“After I received the report and the facts were clear, I took action right away,” Sherrill said, in what may have been a nod to earlier criticism that she didn’t confirm the investigation while it was underway. “Let me be clear: all credible allegations of misconduct must be fully investigated and addressed. In my administration, we are committed to doing what is right, not what is politically expedient.”
The investigation found Caldwell hit on a female staffer’s friend, and when she turned him down, he told the staffer that ambitious women like them needed a man in a position to help them, “but you young women are looking for young sperm.”
Caldwell denied making the comments, “but we did not find his denial credible,” the report said.
Replacing Caldwell
Sherrill did not have the power to fire Caldwell, so his resignation prevents potential impeachment proceedings in Trenton. The governor has 45 days to pick his replacement.
In the meantime, New Jersey Senate President Nicholas Scutari will lead the state in her absence. Sherrill traveled to campaign for Democrats in congressional races in other states earlier in the summer, leaving Caldwell in charge. But she stopped after the investigation became public knowledge.
Sherrill said she spoke to Caldwell on Thursday and texted with him on Friday, and that he resigned to let her administration continue with its agenda amid “all of the attacks from the federal government on affordability, voting rights.”
Caldwell’s attorney, Thomas Calcagni, said in a statement late Friday that his client continues to dispute the allegations in the report and would be exploring “all legal remedies” to contest its findings.
“We continue to forcefully challenge the report. Dr. Caldwell’s resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings,” Calcagni said.
As fragments of the allegations leaked out over the weeks, some of Caldwell’s friends and allies shared messages of support about his character and record of service. And while he did not speak publicly as news of the investigation surfaced, a May letter he wrote to the ethics commission forcefully denying the claims — and alleging racism — was leaked to media.
On Friday, a group of self-described Black “faith, civic, and community leaders” commended his decision to resign.
“By choosing to step down and ending this controversy, he has put the interests of the people of New Jersey and the work of our state ahead of himself,” the group said in a statement, which included U.S. Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D., Mercer), New Jersey Democratic Committee Chair LeRoy Jones, among others.
Democratic state legislators remained largely quiet before Caldwell announced his resignation, but many were relieved to see Caldwell step down.
Assemblymember Anthony Angelozzi, a Burlington County Democrat, said he was “appalled” with the findings of the report.
“The idea of using your government position for personal benefit and harassing women, as someone who has staff members who are female and a daughter, I wouldn’t want to put any woman in a compromised position like that,” he said.
Assemblymember Balivir Singh floated another Burlington County Democrat, State Sen. Troy Singleton, as an ideal replacement for Caldwell.
“You look for a person with integrity … and I would think my senator is the best,” Singh said.
As lieutenant governor, Caldwell served a dual role as the state’s top election official. With his resignation less than 40 days before the midterm election, Sherrill appointed Acting Comptroller Shirley Emehelu to serve as secretary of state on an acting basis.
“For months at this point, the Department of State team has been hard at work preparing for the upcoming elections in partnership with local and county election officials. I will make sure their work proceeds as planned,” Emehelu said.
The investigation into Caldwell was conducted by former Attorney General Christopher Porrino — who worked under former Republican Gov. Chris Christie — and his law firm. The probe had been going on since at least May.
Road crews had begun removing Caldwell’s name from state signs on I-95 as of Friday, but the scandal is still likely to dominate New Jersey politics for the foreseeable future.
Christine Giordano Hanlon, chair of the New Jersey GOP, called Sherrill’s handling of the investigation a “failure.”
“Caldwell’s resignation is not accountability for everything that happened before it,” she said. “There are many more questions that will need to be answered.”
‘Long-term concerning behavior’ outlined in report
Sherrill said the report “lays out a pattern and practice of long-term concerning behavior.” She said her decision shows the “culture change” she has pushed for in Trenton.
“What was so important to me was to make sure that if there are substantiated claims of sexual harassment and ethics violations, that I, as the leader of the government, handle that,” she said.
“There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug,” she said. “You can speak to numerous people who’ve worked in the statehouse for decades who felt this day would never come, that allegations would never be taken seriously, action would never be taken, and victims would just have to either quit their job or move on.”
According to the report, less than a month after being spoken to and given training on workplace conduct and ethics, and four days after he was told about the investigation, Caldwell tried to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating.
Caldwell’s attorney said the lieutenant governor forwarded the employee’s resume and did not disclose the two had a personal relationship.
The report also details comments Caldwell allegedly made about wanting a “first lady.” One staffer said he asked her to find him someone and another recalled him suggesting that he would need a wife in order to run for governor and to let him know if she comes across someone suitable. Caldwell admitted to making comments to staffers about wanting a “first lady” but said he wasn’t serious and other people in the office made similar kinds of jokes, the report said.
He also repeatedly made comments about staffers having “executive appearance,” which came across to some staffers as a judgment on women’s physical attractiveness. Caldwell said the term was about how both men and women carry themselves, not physical appearance, the report said.
Caldwell repeatedly brought personal guests to ticketed events without clearing it with the ethics officer and without paying for the extra tickets, a practice that continued even after warnings, attending an ethics training, and being told about the investigation, the report said. His attorney said when Caldwell “learned that reimbursement was appropriate in one particular situation, he reimbursed $175 for the event.”
He was also accused of providing his business card to women he wanted to date, but he said in his May letter that he gives his business card to more men than women.
“I have never asked anyone out on a date, ‘hit on,’ or pursued anyone romantically while conducting official business as Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State,” he said at the time.
Staff writers Susan K. Livio, Sarah Nicell, and Lacey Latch contributed reporting.
